scope: Independent source/code reading and standard-library hash/token arithmetic only. No production imports, parses, meshes, matrix assemblies or solves.

protocol.mesh_count_qualification: The .52 mandatory property break adds one interval. Counts are source-derived expectations to be checked during execution, not recovered historical forty-node coordinates.
protocol.base: Cold stationary loaded equilibrium with the literal distributed mass and gravity for both orientations.
protocol.reference_precision: Compare every raw real and imaginary token separately at its exact decimal half-last-place interval. Decimal(str(predicted)) is the declared scalar convention; no zero snapping, absolute-value conversion or frequency-only acceptance.

root_selection.positive_predicate: imaginary_component > 0; retain all other roots separately and report near-real/zero ambiguity rather than silently removing them.
root_selection.selection: Sort returned positive-imaginary roots by ascending imaginary component; pair the first7 to native rows1–7. Use original return index only to make a deterministic display tie; an unresolved tie does not establish branch identity.
root_selection.conjugate_witness: For each selected positive root, require a distinct returned negative-imaginary root near its complex conjugate. Report both original indices, both unmodified complex values and the normalized conjugacy defect. Require a one-to-one witness assignment; ambiguous matches fail the selection check.

proposed_conjugacy_diagnostic.scope: Prospective numerical pairing gate aligned with the current selected-cluster scale; not recovered ASWING tolerance, not a root error bound, and never a replacement for original print intervals.

root_selection.insufficient_roots: Retain missing/unavailable target slots and the failed selection check; no change of count, shift, mesh, density or target ordering.
root_selection.local_scope_limitation: Twenty roots nearest a shift are not a complete finite-spectrum census. No proof identifies the archived seven as the globally lowest seven or supplies native mode shapes. This is a qualified ordinal local-spectrum comparison, not historical branch tracking. A complete dense census is not required by the published shifted algorithm.

citations.excerpt:
This menu permits the determination of vibration frequencies, damping 
ratios, and corresponding mode vectors for perturbations taken about the 
current target point, which is any nonlinearly-deformed operating point 
state computed previously in OPER.  If no operating points were computed, 
then the unloaded geometry at zero lift is used as the base state.

citations.claim: Real eigenvalue part describes growth/decay, imaginary part frequency.
citations.excerpt:
Negative damping, indicated by a positive real eigenvalue component, 
indicates instability.  The imaginary component (frequency) and the 
eigenmode associated with that eigenvalue indicates the rate and type 
of instability involved.  Typical instabilities correspond to flight 
dynamics instabilities (e.g. spiral instability), or structural 
instabilities (e.g. flutter).

citations.excerpt:

 Enter shift  sigma,omega:   -0.010000    0.000000

citations.claim: Returned roots are local to the requested shift.
citations.excerpt:
The shift  sigma,omega  give the location in the eigenvalue plane in
whose vicinity the eigenvalues are to be computed.  This shift location
will depend on which eigenvalues are being sought.  Typically, the
algorithm will return the specified number of eigenvalues which 
lie closest to the shift location.

citations.claim: A restrained configuration permits a zero shift; the proposed nonzero default shift remains a fixed prospective choice.
citations.excerpt:
NOTE: If an aircraft in free-flight is being analyzed, then a shift of 
exactly 0,0 cannot be used, since the algorithm creates an LU-decomposition 
of the shifted system Jacobian, which is singular at the origin due to
the presence of zero-frequency rigid-body motion modes.  For restrained 
configurations (e.g. wing clamped in wind tunnel), using the 0,0 shift 
is permissible.

citations.claim: The guide recommends20–30 near-origin roots for an initial spectrum survey; count20 is selected from this advice before results.
citations.excerpt:
When the eigenmode analysis is performed the first time, the eigenmode
distribution is often not very well known.  In this case one would choose
a relatively large number of eigenvalues to be computed (20-30, say), 
and give a shift relatively near 0,0.  This can be an expensive computation,
but will give an indication of what shifts are appropriate for what modes,
which can be used for subsequent analyses with fewer eigenvalues specified.

citations.excerpt:
13.3    Eigenmode  analyses

We  now  consider (131)  for  the unforced case,  with δu = 0.  We  assume a perturbation solution  of
the form
                                                       δx(t)  =  ˆx  exp(λt)
which simpliﬁes (131) to

                                                         A ˆx    =    M ˆxλ                                                               (144)
Eigenvalues  and  eigenvectors  (or  eigenmodes)  are  nontrivial  solutions λk,vk  to  the  unforced  per-
turbed system (144),

                                                       A vk    =    M vkλk                                                            (145)

where k = 1, 2...  is  the solution  mode index.  For  each  eigenvalue λk,  it  is also  useful to  determine
the system’s left-eigenvector wk  from

                                                      w∗k A    =    w∗k Mλk                                                            (146)

where ( )∗ denotes the complex transpose operation (transpose together with complex conjugation).


13.3.1     Eigenmode  computation

The eigenvalues λk  and corresponding eigenvectors  vk  are generated  by recasting system (145) in
the equivalent “shifted power-iteration” form.

                                                  H vk    =    vkνk                                                                        (147)

                                                      H    ≡    [A −µM]−1 M                                                      (148)
                                                      νk    ≡         1λk −µ                                                                     (149)

citations.claim: Largest inverse roots are nearest to the shift; one shifted LU is reused. Left inverse iteration and mass biorthogonality follow.
citations.excerpt:
An  Arnoldi  iteration  method  using H  will  converge  to  the  largest  |νk|,  which  corresponds  to  the
λk  which  is  closest  to the shift µ  in  the complex  plane.  The corresponding eigenvector  vk  is  also
obtained  as  a by-product.  Hence,  one can  selectively  choose µ  to focus  the search  on any  nearby
eigenvalues.  Typically, one would choose µ  ≃ 0 + 0i to search for low-frequency modes such as the
phugoid  and  spiral  modes.   Similarly,  one  would  choose µ  =  0 +iω  to  search  weakly-damped  or
weakly-unstable  (e.g.  ﬂutter) modes  at  an  anticipated  frequency ω.  ASWING  currently  employs
the ARPACK [3] sparse-system eigenvalue package to rapidly compute the eigenpairs.  The matrix
inversion  in  (148)  is  implemented  via  LU  factorization.   This  is  performed  only  once,  and  only
back-substitution operations are required for all subsequent Arnoldi iterations.
The left-eigenvector  wk  corresponding to each λk, vk  pair is obtained  via inverse power iteration.
Starting with a random vector  ˜w0, one iteration step is executed as follows:

                                              w′    =    [AT −λ∗kMT ]−1{          MT ˜wi}                                         (150)

                                           ˜wi+1    =          w′w′∗ M vk                                                                          (151)

The matrix inversion in (150) is implemented via a complex LU factorization, performed once and
then  re-used  for  each  iteration.  The factored  matrix  is  very  nearly  singular,  making  w′  typically
very large.  But because of the normalization operation (151), the  ˜w0, ˜w1... wk sequence converges
stably.  In fact,  convergence  is  extremely  rapid, with only  2  or 3  iterations  being needed  to reach
machine  zero  accuracy.  The normalization  operation  (151)  also  makes  the  resulting  set  of  vk,wk
pairs satisfy the following M-orthonormality condition.

citations.claim: Current Arnoldi uses standard mode1, identity metric, largest inverse magnitude, deterministic starting vector, tolerance1e-11 and shifted-solve backward gate1e-10.
citations.excerpt:
settings = dict(factorizations=1, operator_applications=0,
        maximum_solve_backward_error=0., solve_backward_gate=1e-10,
        retained_dimension=n, arpack_mode=1, bmat='I', which='LM',
        tolerance=1e-11, subspace_dimension=min(n, max(2*count+1, 20)),
        maximum_iterations=max(500, 30*n), starting_vector='deterministic linspace(1,2)',
        factorization='sparse complex LU', mass_rank_reduction=False)

    def apply(vector):
        rhs = m@vector
        result = factor.solve(rhs)
        settings['operator_applications'] += 1
        denominator = matrix_norm*np.linalg.norm(result)+np.linalg.norm(rhs)
        backward = np.linalg.norm(matrix@result-rhs)/max(denominator, np.finfo(float).tiny)
        if not np.all(np.isfinite(result)) or not np.isfinite(backward) or backward > settings['solve_backward_gate']:
            raise AnalysisError('The shifted modal linear solve fails its original-matrix residual check; inspect the shift and scaling.')
        settings['maximum_solve_backward_error'] = max(settings['maximum_solve_backward_error'], float(backward))
        return result

    operator = LinearOperator(a.shape, matvec=apply, dtype=complex)
    try:
        inverse, vectors = eigs(operator, k=count, which=settings['which'],
            tol=settings['tolerance'], ncv=settings['subspace_dimension'],
            maxiter=settings['maximum_iterations'], v0=np.linspace(1., 2., n).astype(complex))
    except ArpackNoConvergence as exc:
        raise AnalysisError('Shift-and-invert modes did not converge; change shift/count or use the dense solve.') from exc
    if (not np.all(np.isfinite(inverse)) or
            np.any(abs(inverse) <= 100*np.finfo(float).eps*max(np.max(abs(inverse)), 1.))):
        raise AnalysisError('The Arnoldi search includes unresolved infinite or very distant roots; reduce count or move the shift.')
    values = shift+1/inverse
    order = np.argsort(abs(values-shift), kind='stable')
    return values[order], vectors[:, order], settings

citations.claim: Fixed source vacuum/still-air requires no FlightCondition, zero motion, no controller/operating constraints and explicit still-air density.
Stationary apparent inertia uses normal thin-strip mass and span-pitch inertia; Xax=.5 makes the midchord arm zero.
citations.excerpt:
def source_apparent_wrench(frame, chord, xax, density, acceleration, angular_acceleration):
    """Per-unit-length thin-strip reaction, in body axes, at stationary base.

    Input chord is already measured in the local airfoil c/n plane. Xax is
    its structural-axis fraction. The real-mass Eq.80 segment correction is
    not a fluid inertia term and is deliberately absent here.
    """
    c, s, n = frame[..., 0], frame[..., 1], frame[..., 2]
    chord = np.asarray(chord)
    arm = ((.5-np.asarray(xax))*chord)[..., None]*c
    mass = density*np.pi/4*chord**2
    normal_acceleration = np.sum((acceleration+np.cross(angular_acceleration, arm))*n, axis=-1)
    force = -(mass*normal_acceleration)[..., None]*n
    moment = np.cross(arm, force)-(mass*chord**2/32*np.sum(s*angular_acceleration, axis=-1))[..., None]*s
    return force, moment
